_note: Before-and-after quiz. Form A before the game, form B after: same eight concepts, different wording and scenarios. Draft for Micah to verify. Option order shuffled with a fixed seed so correct answers are spread across A to D.

A.q: An insurer's liabilities are longer (more rate-sensitive) than its assets. Interest rates fall by 1 percentage point. What happens to its surplus?

options.D: It depends only on stock prices

A.q: Competitors start offering annuities that pay much more than ours because market rates jumped. What should we expect?

options.A: Our annuities become more valuable to keep
options.B: Nothing, surrenders are not linked to rates
options.C: More policyholders cash out (surrender), so we need cash

A.q: Credit spreads widen sharply, but none of our bond issuers defaults. Which statement is true?

options.B: Bond prices fall; if we hold to maturity and nobody defaults, much of that can come back
options.C: We have a permanent loss on every bond
options.D: We have no loss at all

A.q: We wrote guarantees on variable annuities. The stock market falls 20%. What happens?
A bank owes us money on a hedge and then fails. When is our loss smallest?

options.A: When we collected collateral daily and spread hedges across several banks
options.B: When the hedge had grown very valuable
options.D: When we used one bank and took no collateral

B.q: Our assets have a duration of 6 years and our liabilities 10 years, both about the same size. Which rate move hurts us?
Rates fall and our annuities now credit more than new products on the market. What happens to surrenders?

options.B: They always stay exactly the same
options.C: They tend to fall: staying is attractive
options.D: They are forced to zero by law

options.A: A bond price drop caused by wider spreads
options.B: A bond issuer defaulting and paying back only part of the money

B.q: Why do insurers buy put options against the stock market?

options.B: To bet that stocks will rise
options.D: To offset the extra cost of guarantees when stocks fall

B.q: Our swaps lose value when rates rise, and they are collateralized daily. Rates jump. What happens?

options.D: We must post cash collateral now, even though the loss is only on paper

confidence.text: I can explain what a rate mismatch (duration gap) is and which way it hurts.
I can explain why surrenders rise when interest rates climb.
I can explain the difference between a spread move and a default.
I can explain how stock-market guarantees react when markets fall.
I can explain why collateral matters when a dealer fails.

A.q: Why does an insurer keep a cash buffer even though cash earns little?

options.C: Regulators require all assets in cash
options.D: To pay surrenders and margin calls without selling bonds at a discount in a stressed market

A.q: What is the main trade-off of hedging foreign bonds with currency forwards?

options.B: It removes all risk for free
options.D: It protects against a stronger dollar but costs a little every quarter

A.q: A company asks us to take over its pension plan. What do we take on?

options.A: Long-dated promises to retirees plus premium to invest, which uses capital

B.q: Markets freeze and we must raise cash quickly. Which asset can usually be sold with the smallest discount?
We hedge 100% of our foreign bonds against the dollar. What did we give up?

options.B: The quarterly cost of the hedge, and any gain if the dollar had weakened

B.q: After accepting a pension deal, what should we usually do to stay matched?

options.C: Lengthen our assets or add rate protection, because the new promises are long

confidence.text: I can weigh the cost of a hedge against the risk it removes.
